splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over Auer/Kisor deference to agency interpretations when construing ambiguous provisions that carry criminal consequences, such as Sentencing Guidelines enhancements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's or an agency's interpretation of an ambiguous guideline or regulation that expands criminal liability, or whether the rule of lenity should resolve the ambiguity in the defendant's favor. This matters because it determines whether agencies can effectively broaden criminal punishment through regulatory interpretation.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity prevails over agency deference (Auer/Chevron/Kisor) when interpreting ambiguous provisions with criminal consequences, requiring ambiguity to be resolved in the defendant's favor rather than deferring to the government's interpretation.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference (under Auer/Kisor/Stinson) can override the rule of lenity, allowing the government's interpretation of ambiguous guidelines to expand criminal liability.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1) of the First Step Act's safety-valve provision is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether a defendant must meet all three criminal-history disqualifiers in § 3553(f)(1) to be ineligible for safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any one is sufficient. This directly affects mandatory minimum sentencing for drug offenses and produces disparate sentences depending on where a defendant is prosecuted.

positions.label: 'And' means conjunctive (all three required)
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' conjunctively.

positions.label: 'And' means disjunctive (any one disqualifies)
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which adds inchoate offenses (conspiracy, aiding and abetting, attempt) to the definition of 'controlled substance offense' for career-offender purposes, is a valid and binding interpretation of the guideline.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary expanding 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy is entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor, or whether the guideline text unambiguously excludes such offenses. This affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions qualify as career offenders under the Guidelines.

positions.label: Commentary is valid and binding
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and is entitled to controlling weight, so inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition beyond its plain meaning, so it is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state's drug schedules are broader than the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether USSG § 4B1.2(b)'s definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance to be controlled under federal law or whether state-law controlled substances suffice. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions involving substances not on federal schedules.

positions.label: State schedules suffice
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include state law offenses regardless of whether the substance is federally scheduled, finding no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation.

positions.label: Must match federal schedules
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act, applying a categorical approach.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the First Step Act's non-retroactive anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement in U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) validly authorizes such relief.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, particularly the First Step Act's elimination of mandatory stacked § 924(c) sentences, can support compassionate release. Some circuits hold that the Commission exceeded its authority in adopting § 1B1.13(b)(6), while others allow consideration of such changes. This affects hundreds of prisoners serving decades-long stacked sentences.

positions.label: Non-retroactive change cannot support relief
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether offered alone or in combination with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, and that the Sentencing Commission exceeded its authority in § 1B1.13(b)(6).

positions.label: Non-retroactive change can support relief
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in law, including the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment, may be considered as part of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, and that the Sentencing Commission's § 1B1.13(b)(6) policy statement is valid.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must use habeas corpus (28 U.S.C. § 2241) as the exclusive remedy to challenge BOP decisions affecting the duration or conditions of confinement, or whether civil rights actions (e.g., Bivens) are also available.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists over whether challenges to BOP decisions—such as denial of early transfer to prerelease custody under the First Step Act—must proceed as habeas petitions or may be brought as civil rights claims. The Supreme Court has repeatedly noted but not resolved this question since Preiser v. Rodriguez (1973), and the split affects federal prisoners' access to remedies and procedural protections.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive for duration challenges
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner challenges the fact or duration of confinement, including BOP decisions on earned time credits or prerelease custody, habeas corpus is the sole federal remedy.

positions.label: Civil rights actions also available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may bring civil rights actions (such as Bivens or § 1983 claims) to challenge conditions or terms of confinement even when the relief sought could affect release dates, as long as they are not directly challenging the validity of the conviction or sentence.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment order (attorney's fees in criminal cases) is governed by the civil appeal deadline (30 days) or the criminal appeal deadline (14 days).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees, though arising from a criminal case, is a civil matter for purposes of the appellate filing deadline. The majority of circuits treat it as civil (30-day deadline), but some have applied the criminal deadline. This affects whether appeals from Hyde Amendment denials are timely.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, and therefore the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: United States v. Manchester Farming Partnership

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that since the Hyde Amendment motion arises in a criminal case, the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between a Chapter 13 filing and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. This split affects debtors' incentives to convert and the distribution of assets to creditors.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that under § 348(f)(1)(A) and § 541(a), the broad definition of 'property of the estate' means that post-petition appreciation in property value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that under the structure and legislative history of § 348(f), post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor, not the estate, to preserve the incentive for good-faith conversion.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may impose a revocation sentence for supervised release that is expressly based on punishment for the underlying violation, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to the goals of deterrence, public protection, and rehabilitation.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the purposes of a supervised-release revocation sentence may include retributive punishment for the violation or must be limited to forward-looking goals. The Sixth Circuit allows courts to expressly punish defendants for violations, while other circuits prohibit purely punitive revocation sentences. This affects the length and rationale of sentences imposed at revocation hearings.

positions.label: Punishment permitted
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release conditions, and that the purposes of revocation sentencing include retribution.

positions.label: Punishment not permitted
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences for supervised release violations must be based on forward-looking goals like deterrence, public protection, and rehabilitation, not on retributive punishment for the violation itself.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether actuarial assumptions used to calculate an employer's withdrawal liability from a multiemployer pension plan must be established before the statutory measurement date or may be selected afterward. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be determined by the end of the prior plan year (the statutory measurement date), providing employers with greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that an actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing plans to use updated information in calculating withdrawal liability.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects revocation proceedings for thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is tolled while a supervisee is a fugitive, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release during absconding, and that the term expires as stated in the judgment regardless of whether the supervisee flees.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing successive motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: A 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1)—which prohibits relitigation of claims presented in a prior habeas application—applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions. If it applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than § 2255(h) alone would impose, categorically barring previously raised claims.

positions.label: § 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims applies to successive § 2255 motions by federal prisoners, in addition to the requirements of § 2255(h).

positions.label: § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions, so federal prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law for successive motions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits have disagreed on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures such as mail-in ballot deadlines, with some circuits granting broad candidate standing and others requiring a more particularized showing of injury. This affects the ability to challenge election administration rules before an election occurs.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge election rules that allegedly dilute lawful votes or alter the competitive landscape, even before an election takes place.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates lack Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to ballot-counting rules absent a concrete, particularized injury beyond generalized competitive concerns.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether orders denying motions to seal medical records qualify as collateral orders subject to immediate appeal under 28 U.S.C. § 1291. The D.C. Circuit has held that medical privacy constitutes a value of 'high order' warranting immediate review, while other circuits have taken narrower views of the collateral order doctrine in similar contexts.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denials of motions to seal medical records are immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of high order that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denials of motions to seal are not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine, as the privacy interest can be adequately vindicated through other means or on appeal from final judgment.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: In re Roman Catholic Archbishop of Portland

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: Circuits have applied different standards for evaluating discrimination claims in business and hospitality contexts. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve the Second Circuit's approach, suggesting a circuit split on liability standards, available remedies, and the scope of protections for customers in service industries.

positions.label: Broader liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a broader standard for discrimination claims in hospitality or business establishments, potentially allowing claims based on a wider range of conduct.

positions.label: Narrower liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a narrower standard requiring a more specific showing of discriminatory conduct before liability attaches in hospitality or business settings.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether state laws categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violate the Equal Protection Clause, and what level of scrutiny applies to such classifications.
splits.description: Circuits are beginning to divide on the constitutionality of state laws that categorically prohibit transgender athletes from competing on teams consistent with their gender identity. This split implicates the level of scrutiny applicable to sex-based and transgender classifications and whether as-applied challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.

positions.label: Laws likely violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that categorical bans on transgender women in women's sports likely violate the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender individuals who have medically mitigated their sex-based biological advantages.

positions.label: Laws are constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that such laws are a permissible exercise of state authority to maintain fair competition in women's sports based on biological sex differences.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
